main.title: Nintendo
main.subtitle: Change the Tools, Keep Inventing Games
main.summary: On September 23, 1889, according to Nintendo's corporate documentation, Fusajiro Yamauchi founded the Kyoto business that would become Nintendo, devoted to the production and sale of hanafuda cards.

cards.heading: The Kyoto playing-card business
cards.text: Fusajiro Yamauchi founded the Kyoto business that became Nintendo on 23 September 1889. It produced and sold hanafuda, Japanese playing cards used for several games. As demand grew, Yamauchi hired assistants to increase production. Playing cards formed the company's first business, long before its mechanical toys, electronic games and consoles.

cards.heading: Hanafuda: pictures on playing cards
cards.text: Hanafuda (lit. 'flower cards') are a type of Japanese playing cards. They are typically smaller than Western playing cards, only 5.4 by 3.2 centimetres (2.1 by 1.3 in), but thicker and stiffer. On the face of each card is a depiction of plants, tanzaku ('paper strips'), animals, birds, or man-made objects. One single card depicts a human. The back side is usually plain, without a pattern or design of any kind, and traditionally colored either red or black. Hanafuda are used to play a variety of games including Koi-Koi and Hachi-Hachi.

cards.heading: Gunpei Yokoi and the extending Ultra Hand
cards.text:
Ultra Hand is a toy that was manufactured by Nintendo in the late 1960s. It was created in 1966 by Gunpei Yokoi, who later designed the Love Tester, the D-pad, the Game & Watch, the Game Boy, and the WonderSwan.

Ultra Hand consists of several criss-cross-connected plastic elements, and operates on the "lazy tongs" pantograph principle. One end of the Ultra Hand has scissor-like handles and is operated like scissors, extending when the handles are pinched together and retracting when they are parted.  On the other end of the Ultra Hand are two bowl-shaped grips with which ball-like objects can be gripped when the Ultra Hand is fully extended. Three colored balls were included in the Ultra Hand package, along with stands on which the balls can rest.

cards.heading: Color TV-Game 6 and 15
cards.text: In 1977, Nintendo released the Color TV-Game 6 and Color TV-Game 15, two consoles jointly developed with Mitsubishi Electric. The numbers in the console names indicate the number of games included in each. They were the start of the Color TV-Game line of console.

cards.heading: Game & Watch: a game and a clock
cards.text: In addition to the arcade games, Nintendo was testing the consumer handheld video game market with the Game & Watch. It is a line of handheld electronic games produced by Nintendo from 1980 to 1991. Created by Gunpei Yokoi, each Game & Watch features a single game to be played on an LCD screen in addition to a clock or an alarm. It is the earliest Nintendo product to garner major success, with 43.4 million units sold worldwide.

cards.heading: Famicom and the Nintendo Entertainment System
cards.text: Nintendo launched the cartridge-based Family Computer, or Famicom, in Japan in 1983, selling more than 500,000 units within two months. Reports of games freezing led the company to identify a faulty chip and recall machines from shop shelves. The overseas Nintendo Entertainment System presented the platform in a grey, front-loading case resembling living-room electronics. Nintendo called its cartridges Game Paks and the console a Control Deck. R.O.B., a robot-shaped accessory, helped give retailers and households another way to understand the system.

cards.heading: 1989 / Game Boy and Tetris
cards.text: Nintendo released the Game Boy in 1989. Super Mario Land accompanied its launch, while Tetris became another defining part of the handheld's library. Price, durability and widely popular games helped the Game Boy line reach 118 million sales. Super Mario Land alone sold 14 million copies. That same year, Nintendo announced its next home console, the Super Famicom, continuing its handheld and television-based businesses side by side.

cards.heading: 1990 / The Super Famicom generation
cards.text: The Super Famicom was released in Japan in 1990. It sold out across Japan within three days, with 1.6 million units sold by mid-1991. Later in 1991, the Super Famicom was launched in the U.S. as the "Super Nintendo Entertainment System" (SNES), followed by Europe in 1992. Like the NES, the Super Nintendo Entertainment System had high technical specifications for its era. The SNES controller was more ergonomic than that of the NES, as it now had rounded edges and four new buttons, a standard which is evident on many modern controllers today.

cards.heading: 1996 / Learning to move in three dimensions
cards.text: Nintendo 64 brought Nintendo's major home-console series into three-dimensional spaces. Its cartridge format contrasted with the optical discs used by competitors, creating different trade-offs for developers, manufacturing and storage. Super Mario 64 made the controller's analogue stick central to movement. Before building its worlds, Shigeru Miyamoto and the development team concentrated on how Mario should feel to control. Running, jumping and changing direction needed to make sense before the surrounding levels could teach the player what to do with those actions.

cards.heading: 2001 / Game Boy Advance
cards.text: Game Boy Advance extended Nintendo's handheld line while keeping earlier Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges playable. Its wider colour screen and new processor gave developers a different space for games without discarding the existing library. Nintendo also connected the handheld and living-room branches of its business: a link cable let a Game Boy Advance communicate with a GameCube. Compatible games could use the handheld for private information or an additional view, turning the relationship between screens into part of the design.

cards.heading: 2001 / A different shape for the living room
cards.text: GameCube replaced Nintendo's home-console cartridges with small optical discs. Its compact case, carrying handle and distinctive controller gave it a different physical identity from its competitors. The software library included Super Smash Bros. Melee, Super Mario Sunshine, The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker and Metroid Prime. Game Boy Advance connectivity added another approach to multiplayer and second-screen play. The console's commercial difficulties also formed the background to Nintendo's subsequent decision to seek a wider audience with Wii.

cards.heading: 2002 / Satoru Iwata becomes president
cards.text: Satoru Iwata joined Nintendo's corporate planning division after leading HAL Laboratory. In 2002, Hiroshi Yamauchi chose him as Nintendo's next president, the first president outside the founding Yamauchi family. Iwata brought experience as a working programmer as well as a company leader. The DS and Wii years placed reaching new players alongside serving existing fans. His later Iwata Asks interviews also made the work of designers, programmers, artists and hardware engineers visible through conversations about how Nintendo's products were made.

cards.heading: 2004 / Two screens, one new vocabulary
cards.text: Nintendo DS combined a conventional game screen with a second screen that could be touched directly. The stylus made pointing, drawing and writing part of the controller, while the microphone and local wireless connection offered further ways to interact. Games such as Nintendogs and Brain Age reached people who did not necessarily think of themselves as console players. The DS also continued to support familiar kinds of play. Its success depended on that combination: new gestures and audiences alongside a substantial library for existing players.

cards.heading: 2006 / Wii opens the room
cards.text: The Wii Remote took its shape from a familiar household object: the television remote control. Satoru Iwata recalled asking why people readily picked up a TV remote while a game controller could seem intimidating. Pointing and motion sensing gave developers a different set of actions to work with. In Wii Sports, swinging the controller connected a recognisable physical movement to a result on screen. The team still had to communicate each action clearly, but players could begin with gestures they already understood.

cards.heading: 2011 / Depth without glasses
cards.text: Nintendo 3DS retained the DS family's two-screen arrangement but added stereoscopic depth that could be viewed without special glasses. A slider adjusted the strength of that effect or turned it off. The system also added a circle pad, motion sensors and cameras. Its early sales difficulties led Nintendo to reduce the price, after which the platform built a substantial library over several years. It shows a recurring feature of Nintendo's history: introducing a technical idea is only the beginning of making a platform work.

cards.heading: 2012 / Wii U and the second screen
cards.text: Wii U brought high-definition output to Nintendo's home consoles and placed a touchscreen inside its GamePad controller. A game could put different information in the player's hands and on the television, or support play on the controller's screen. The idea proved difficult to communicate, and the console did not match Wii's commercial success. Its games and experiments nevertheless remained significant: several later reached a much larger audience on Switch, and the relationship between home play and a handheld screen remained an important question.

cards.heading: 2017 / One library, at home and away
cards.text: Nintendo Switch joined handheld and television play in a single platform. The tablet-like console could be used on its own or placed in a dock, while its Joy-Con controllers could be attached or removed. The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild launched alongside the system, and Super Mario Odyssey followed in the same year. Instead of maintaining separate handheld and home-console libraries, Nintendo could develop around a shared machine. The change made moving between different places and ways of playing a defining feature of the hardware.

cards.heading: 2024 / The objects become a museum
cards.text: Nintendo Museum in Uji, Kyoto brings together the company's playing cards, toys, electronic games and consoles. The displays follow its changing products, while playable installations and a hanafuda workshop let visitors try some of those ideas themselves. In the official museum tour, Shigeru Miyamoto walks through the collection and explains connections between objects from different periods.

cards.heading: 2025 / Nintendo Switch 2
cards.text: Nintendo Switch 2 continues the hybrid design with a larger display and redesigned magnetic Joy-Con 2 controllers. Its controllers can also be used in a mouse-like way in supported software, adding another gesture to the platform's vocabulary. Backward compatibility keeps much of the original Switch library in reach, while new games explore the successor's capabilities. It belongs to the same long history as the playing cards and mechanical toys: a business repeatedly changing the tools it uses to make games.

main.title: Josef Kates
main.subtitle: Engineer and early game-computing pioneer
main.summary: Josef Kates was born in Vienna on 5 May 1921. His engineering work would include Bertie the Brain and automated traffic signalling.

cards.heading: Josef Kates
cards.text: Josef Kates was a Canadian engineer born Josef Katz in Vienna on 5 May 1921. His work included Bertie the Brain, a digital game-playing machine exhibited in 1950, and an automated traffic-signalling system for Toronto. Both projects put computing in front of a public audience: visitors could challenge Bertie to a game, while road users encountered a system coordinating the city's traffic.

cards.heading: From Vienna to Canada
cards.text: Kates fled Austria after the Nazi annexation in 1938, first reaching Italy and then joining his family in England. Although he enlisted in the British Army, he was interned as an enemy alien and deported to Canada. During almost two years in camps, he worked and studied through McGill University's school programme, placing first in Quebec's examinations. The Canadian government eventually recognised him and other Jewish internees as victims of Nazi aggression. Released in 1942, he moved to Toronto, where he met Lillian Kroch; they married in 1944.

cards.heading: Mathematics and physics
cards.text: Kates attended the Goethe-Realschule in Vienna from 1931 to 1938. During his internment in Canada, he completed McGill University's junior and senior matriculation examinations in 1941. He later studied mathematics and physics at the University of Toronto, earning an honours degree in 1948, a master's degree in applied mathematics in 1949 and a doctorate in physics in 1951.

cards.heading: Radar tubes and UTEC
cards.text: Kates started his career working for the Imperial Optical Company of Toronto in 1942, and was in charge of precision optics for Royal Canadian Navy equipment until he left in 1944. He then spent time working for Rogers Vacuum Tube Company, (now Royal Philips Electronics), for the next four years in the development and manufacturing of radar and radio tubes.  He then began work in 1948 at the University of Toronto Computation Centre, where he participated in the design and building of UTEC, the first pilot model of a computer built in Canada.

cards.heading: Bertie the Brain
cards.text: Kates also built the first digital game playing machine, the 13-foot tall Bertie the Brain, which was exhibited at the 1950 Canadian National Exhibition. The game was a version of Tic-tac-toe, with adjustable difficulty levels. The game machine controlled the lighting of an overhead display to show the progress of the game, and was built using a special electron tube, the Additron Tube, which Kates had invented. The Additron Tube did the work of ten existing radio tubes, reducing the size and complexity of the machine.  With the advent of transistors, which were much smaller and required less power, the tube was not put into commercial use.

cards.heading: Automated traffic control
cards.text: Kates also designed Toronto's automated traffic signalling system in 1954 - the first in the world.

cards.heading: Computer consulting
cards.text: Kates founded and became the President of KCS Ltd in Toronto between 1954 and 1966, which merged with the consulting arm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell & Co. to become Kates, Peat, Marwick & Co. in Canada, with other corporations in the US and the UK, for which he acted as a co-managing partner.  He served as a computer consultant to many Canadian and American firms and organizations. He was involved in the creation of Setak Computer Services Corp. Ltd. (his last name spelled backwards) which was based in Toronto; it offered computer access and consulting based on Burroughs computers, e.g. the B5500. Setak's employee Barry W. Ramer later went on to found Barry W. Ramer & Partners Ltd. and Ramer Data Consulting Ltd. Management Consulting in Calgary Alberta. In 1974 he founded Josef Kates Associates Inc., for which he acted as president.

cards.heading: The Science Council of Canada
cards.text: In 1968, he was appointed to the Science Council of Canada, and served as its chairman from 1975 to 1978. Kates was also chairman, CEO and director of Teleride Sage Ltd. (1977–1996), and IRD Teleride (1996–1997) followed until his retirement.

cards.heading: A continuing interest in transit
cards.text: In 2014, at the age of 93, Kates designed a proposed improvement for Toronto Transit Commission subway system.

cards.heading: Family and later life
cards.text: His wife, Lillian Kroch, died of cancer in 1993 after almost 50 years of marriage. In 1995, Kates married his second wife, Kay Hill. Kates died in Toronto on June 16, 2018.

main.title: Ralph Baer
main.subtitle: A life in games
main.summary: Ralph Baer was born in Germany on 8 March 1922. Decades later, his television-game prototypes would lead to the Magnavox Odyssey.

cards.heading: An inventor born in 1922
cards.text: Ralph Henry Baer (born Rudolf Heinrich Baer; March 8, 1922 – December 6, 2014) was a German-born American inventor, game developer, and engineer.

cards.heading: Television games take shape in the 1960s
cards.text: Baer's Jewish family fled Germany just before World War II and Baer served the American war effort, gaining an interest in electronics shortly thereafter. Through several jobs in the electronics industry, he was working as an engineer at Sanders Associates (now BAE Systems) in Nashua, New Hampshire, when he conceived the idea of playing games on a television screen around 1966. With support of his employers, he worked through several prototypes until he arrived at a "Brown Box" that would later become the blueprint for the first home video game console, licensed by Magnavox as the Magnavox Odyssey. Baer continued to design several other consoles and computer game units, including contributing to design of the Simon electronic game. Baer continued to work in electronics until his death in 2014, with over 150 patents to his name.

cards.heading: A later national honour
cards.text: Baer is considered "the Father of Video Games" due to his many contributions to games and helping to spark the video game industry in the latter half of the 20th century. In February 2006, he was awarded the National Medal of Technology for "his groundbreaking and pioneering creation, development and commercialization of interactive video games, which spawned related uses, applications, and mega-industries in both the entertainment and education realms".

main.title: Takeshi Kitano
main.subtitle: When Beat Takeshi Treated the Famicom Like a Stage
main.summary: Takeshi Kitano was born on January 18, 1947, and is also known in Japan as Beat Takeshi.

cards.heading: When Beat Takeshi Treated the Famicom Like a Stage
cards.text: Takeshi Kitano, also known as Beat Takeshi, was born on 18 January 1947. His career spans comedy, television, acting and film directing. In 1986 he supervised Taito's Famicom action-adventure Takeshi no Chousenjou. The game follows a salaryman whose search for treasure involves work, money, family and deliberately eccentric decisions. Kitano's taste for absurdity reaches beyond the dialogue: the player must perform unusual actions and make choices that disrupt the protagonist's ordinary life.

cards.heading: Before the Famicom, an Author Who Likes Breaking the Format
cards.text: Kitano first became known through the Two Beat comedy duo before moving into television, acting and directing. Abrupt changes of tone and the disruption of expectations recur across that work. His involvement with Taito brought this approach to a home-console game. Takeshi no Chousenjou gave players an unpredictable set of tasks, drawing on the public personality audiences already knew as Beat Takeshi.

cards.heading: A Salaryman Instead of a Hero
cards.text: The protagonist of Takeshi no Chousenjou is a salaryman setting out in search of treasure. Everyday activities become part of the adventure: quitting a job, spending money, visiting bars and singing can all contribute to progress. Taito describes it as an action-adventure supervised by Beat Takeshi. Its satire depends on the things the player is asked to do, turning decisions about work, family and leisure into an increasingly eccentric route through the story.

cards.heading: The Console Asks for Actions That Feel Out of Place
cards.text: The original Famicom version uses features of the Japanese console itself, including the microphone built into the second controller. Some puzzles therefore require actions beyond moving the character and pressing the usual game buttons. Their unusual demands contribute to the game's difficult reputation. They also make the physical console part of the joke: equipment sitting beside the television becomes something the player must consider when looking for a solution.

main.title: Nimrod
main.subtitle: A computer explains itself through a game
main.summary: At the Festival of Britain, a wall of lights invited visitors to play Nim against a machine.

cards.heading: An exhibition challenge
cards.text: Ferranti took a purpose-built Nim-playing machine to the 1951 Festival of Britain. John Bennett proposed the project, and engineer Raymond Stuart-Williams turned the proposal into working hardware. The familiar game gave visitors a way into an unfamiliar subject: automatic computation. A person could make a legal move, wait for the reply and understand the consequence without learning the machine’s circuitry first. Nimrod therefore belonged to an exhibition about technology as well as a history of play. Its public audience was part of the engineering brief, rather than an accidental discovery after construction.

cards.heading: Buttons become numbers
cards.text: Ferranti’s original guide explains how controls represented match heaps. Instead of moving counters by hand, the player pressed a numbered button on the control panel to leave a chosen amount in a heap, then asked the computer to respond. Lamps displayed the position. The arrangement translated a rule into an interface: a button expressed a choice in the game. The same written guide described input, storage and output, using the contest as a practical example of how those parts could work together.

cards.heading: Showing the decision
cards.text: Nimrod could display a sequence of instructions as it selected a move. Illuminated steps and arrows exposed part of the calculation instead of hiding everything behind the answer. This was a different ambition from giving a machine a mysterious personality. Ferranti’s booklet warned that describing computers as brains could make their operation seem unknowable. The game offered an inspectable problem. Visitors might enjoy winning or losing, but the demonstration also invited them to follow how a result was produced. A visible process was part of what Ferranti wanted to sell.

main.title: OXO
main.subtitle: A telephone dial becomes a game controller
main.summary: Sandy Douglas put noughts and crosses on EDSAC, making a familiar contest part of life inside a computing laboratory.

cards.heading: A telephone dial meets a computer
cards.text: OXO is a noughts-and-crosses game made by Cambridge PhD student Alexander 'Sandy' Douglas for the EDSAC research computer, usually dated to 1952. A player entered moves with a rotary telephone dial and followed the board on a small cathode-ray display. They could choose to move first or let the computer begin, making a familiar game playable through the laboratory machine's input and display equipment.

cards.heading: Repurposing the display
cards.text: EDSAC's monitor tubes displayed the contents of parts of its memory. Douglas used that existing equipment to show a noughts-and-crosses board, with the rotary dial providing a way to choose a square. The arrangement connected a visible position to an input and a computer response. The later replica project's simulator preserves this combination, allowing users to enter moves through a simulated telephone dial.

cards.heading: A game inside a research laboratory
cards.text: OXO was available on a research computer inside Cambridge, limiting how many people could encounter it. A visitor or researcher could nevertheless play a complete contest against the machine: choose a square, inspect the new board position and wait for its response. This small laboratory program brought the controls, display and decisions of a recognisable game together on EDSAC.

cards.heading: A shared research machine
cards.text: EDSAC served Cambridge researchers through the work of several contributors. Maurice Wilkes led the project, Bill Renwick directed construction and David Wheeler developed methods that helped people use the computer. Douglas could build and test his game within that shared computing environment. Its display and telephone-dial controls were a particular use of a machine whose wider purpose was to run programs for research.

main.title: Shigeru Miyamoto
main.subtitle: Designing Play as a Form of Curiosity
main.summary: Born on 16 November 1952, Shigeru Miyamoto joined Nintendo in 1977 and helped develop series including Donkey Kong, Super Mario, The Legend of Zelda and Pikmin.

cards.heading: Designing Play as a Form of Curiosity
cards.text: Shigeru Miyamoto was born on 16 November 1952 and joined Nintendo in 1977. As a designer, producer and supervisor, he helped develop Donkey Kong, Super Mario, The Legend of Zelda, Pikmin and other series with Nintendo's teams. His work often begins by testing a simple interaction in a prototype. Jumping, exploring or directing a group of creatures then provides a starting point for characters and worlds, with the controller and the player's actions considered together.

cards.heading: Before the Worlds, the Gesture
cards.text: Miyamoto came to Nintendo with a background in industrial design. Donkey Kong gave him an early opportunity to connect a character's actions with the layout of a game. Mario's jump lets the player cross gaps and avoid barrels, so the placement of platforms and obstacles determines when that action is useful or dangerous. The arcade cabinet also demands clarity: a player needs to recognise the character, understand the threat and begin responding within seconds.

cards.heading: The Level Teaches Without Interrupting
cards.text: In Super Mario Bros., the first Goomba, suspended blocks and gaps introduce the player to Mario's movement. Jumping over an enemy produces a different result from hitting a block or falling into a pit. Growing larger changes how Mario occupies the same space. Later levels combine these familiar elements in more difficult arrangements. Miyamoto and the EAD team's approach lets the player learn through actions and their consequences, with the layout showing where a newly discovered ability might be useful.

cards.heading: Curiosity Must Receive an Answer
cards.text: The Legend of Zelda makes remembering and revisiting places part of progress. A passage may become useful after the player finds a new tool; a suspicious wall encourages an experiment. Miyamoto has described the importance of considering a problem from the player's perspective. The clues, objects and layout need to give discoveries a recognisable logic. Exploration develops as the player learns how the world responds and returns to earlier locations with a better idea of what to try.

cards.heading: The Author Who Works Inside a Team
cards.text: Nintendo's development interviews describe work shared among designers, programmers, artists and musicians. Takashi Tezuka, Toshihiko Nakago, Yoshiaki Koizumi, Koji Kondo and many others discuss and revise ideas with Miyamoto. His role changes between projects, from design to production or supervision. During Super Mario Galaxy 2, exchanges with Koizumi and the team addressed the game's structure, actions and amount of narrative material. These conversations show specific problems being worked through by a group.

cards.heading: When the Controller Enters the Design
cards.text: Miyamoto's work also extends to hardware. In an interview about the Super Famicom, he recalled helping its industrial designer with the shape of the Japanese and European console and its controller. Rounded forms affect how a pad sits in the hands, while shoulder buttons and button placement change which combinations are comfortable to use. Those decisions give software teams a set of possible gestures before they build a game's actions around them.

cards.heading: First the Structure, Then the Character
cards.text: Nintendo's EAD interviews describe a process of looking for a new game structure before deciding its characters and appearance. Pikmin gives a concrete example of the possibilities involved. The player directs a small population, organises tasks and manages limited time. Commands can move dozens of creatures efficiently, while their fragility makes mistakes immediately visible and audible. The relationship between the player and the group gives routine planning an emotional consequence.

cards.heading: A face inside a grid
cards.text: Moustache, cap and overalls become a signature, but they also solve the problem of making a body readable in a few pixels. The moustache defines the face, the cap simplifies the hair and the overalls distinguish arms from torso. Miyamoto turns a graphical constraint into personality. Before becoming an icon, Mario must make his actions immediately understandable.

cards.heading: Every path can hide another
cards.text: In 1990, Super Mario World accompanies the Super Famicom's Japanese debut. Miyamoto and Nintendo's team retain the immediate pleasure of jumping but give it a more branching geography: secret exits, alternative routes and a partnership with Yoshi. The world does more than connect levels. It promises hidden possibilities and invites us back to places we thought we had finished.

cards.heading: Mario moves through three dimensions
cards.text: Super Mario 64 has been described as a 3D platformer and action-adventure game in which the player controls the titular character Mario through various courses. Mario's abilities are far more diverse than in previous games. He can walk, run, jump, crouch, crawl, climb, swim, kick, grab objects, and punch using the game controller's analog stick and buttons. He can execute special jumps by combining a regular jump with other actions, including the double and triple jumps, long jump, backflip, and wall jump. The player can adjust the camera—operated by a Lakitu broadcasting Mario—and toggle between first-person and third-person view.

cards.heading: A world held in your hands
cards.text: Gunpei Yokoi's development group created the Game Boy. Its place alongside Nintendo's home consoles shows how the company's hardware and software work extended into different settings. Portable play meant designing around hands, available light, batteries and short intervals. The system's identity came from the interaction between that equipment and the games made for it, bringing together skills from across Nintendo's development teams.

cards.heading: Honouring a way of making us play
cards.text: In 2010, BAFTA awarded Miyamoto its Fellowship, the organisation's highest individual honour. The award recognised his career in game development, including work that made jumping, exploring and experimenting familiar activities for a large audience. His games also reflect the contributions of the many Nintendo designers, programmers, artists and musicians who developed them.

cards.heading: The Order of Culture recognises game development
cards.text: On October 23, 2026, Japan announces Shigeru Miyamoto as a recipient of the Order of Culture, the first game developer selected for the honour. The award recognises outstanding contributions to Japanese culture and science. At a press conference held at Nintendo's Kyoto headquarters the previous day, Miyamoto describes the recognition as belonging to the many people with whom he has made games, rather than to one creator alone. His selection places game development within Japan's highest cultural honours, alongside achievements in other arts and sciences. The conferment ceremony is scheduled for Culture Day, November 3.
